🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.60% (intraday, 7-year +9bp). At trading day 40 (last close) it was +0.40% against a five-campaign average of -1.23% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.77%. The 10-year is +10bp since the hike vs a +20bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 790bp against a five-year average of 420bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is holding: single-B +10bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.34 → 0.65 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+6bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,164bp, -3bp since 2026-11-11, 30bp under the Oct 15 record and 712bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 79.8 (15.0%, -1.6pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 144bp, Oracle 306bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -22%, NBIS -25%, IREN -40% vs NVDA -24%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 27 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -14.4% vs -18.9% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 32% in 3m, 38% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 56%. 6m odds +1.8pp since 2026-11-11. Triggered signposts: Basket names >20% off high.
  • Stocks: Big US indexes slipped; small companies fell hardest as borrowing costs jumped.
  • FX: The dollar firmed a little; the euro and yen barely moved.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq sit below short-term trend lines but above long-term ones.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lender premiums are calm overall, but the riskiest junk bonds stay badly stressed.

The PM story is rates. US Treasuries sold off hard: the 2Y rose 14.37bp to 4.8814%, the 10Y rose 13.51bp to 5.1271% and the 30Y rose 9.97bp to 5.4521%. Gilts (+7.7bp to 5.299%) and Bunds (+3.1bp to 3.347%) followed. Equities absorbed the move unevenly. The S&P 500 fell -0.35% to 7592.4, the Nasdaq -0.39% to 25366.09 and the Dow -0.36% to 52297.09, while the rate-sensitive Russell 2000 fell -1.66% to 2799.06. VIX rose 1.21 to 18.7. Europe ended slightly higher (SX5E +0.09%, STOXX 600 +0.14%, FTSE +0.25%), while the Nikkei fell -0.70%. Brent jumped +3.28% to 95.8 and WTI +2.55% to 88.74, which adds an energy-inflation edge to the yield move. Silver fell -3.22% and copper -1.49%. Sentiment is cautious rather than panicked: IG and HY index spreads were unchanged at 0.88% and 3.20%. Under the surface, junk stress is still concentrated at the bottom of the quality ladder. The Caa–B gap is 790bp against a 5-year average of about 420bp. That puts it at the 99.8th percentile of the past 5 years, after widening +218bp over 3 months, and it is the widest since April 2020 (the FRED CCC–B cross-check is 983bp, 99.1st percentile). So far it has not clearly spread. Single-B widened only +10bp over a month and Ba was flat (0bp). IG was 88bp, +6bp over the month. The warning sign is the 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily moves. It has climbed from 0.338 three months ago to 0.649 now, closing in on its 5-year median of 0.692, so CCC and single-B are moving together more often. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. The tech phase model still reads Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 27 days after the 2026-10-06 peak, with the basket down -14.41%. One signpost has triggered: 57.14% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, past the 50% line. SOX is -28.21% from its 52-week high, 1.79 points from the -30% signpost. The model's 6-month odds of Phase 2-or-3 rose 1.8pp versus yesterday. AI credit is calmer: CoreWeave 5Y CDS is about 1,164bp, 30bp below its 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and down about 20bp on the week, and Nvidia CDS is 143.8bp. Both are descriptive only.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.68 vol points (48th percentile of the 67 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.4 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 89bp (flatter by 1bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (103bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 42 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 66/100 — Persistent, not accelerating sharply. Core gauges are stuck around 2.6–3.1%: Core PCE 3.12, Core CPI 2.6, Median CPI 2.8, Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.9, Sticky CPI 3.09. Most underlying measures are 'rising' or 'flat' and none is 'falling', which the computed Core-Trend Sub-Score (shown separately) reflects. Breadth is the bigger worry: the Dallas distribution shows 52.6% of the PCE basket inflating above 3% (16.6% above 10%), against 25.6% falling (computed). Flexible CPI at 6.2% and the oil spike keep headline risk tilted up, which fits markets pricing a December hike. Wage pressure is modest: AHE 3.1, and ECI at 0.8 is likely a quarterly rather than year-on-year figure. Breakevens are anchored (5y 2.3176, 1y 2.0945), so this is sticky inflation, not de-anchoring.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.

Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Today's tech basket sits -14.41% from its 2026-10-06 peak, 27 days in. On the same day of the 2000 bust that basket was -18.9%, so this drawdown is milder so far. The 2000 analog says early drops with calm credit can stay contained. The model's 1-month odds keep Phase 1 at 0.818, and the 24-month P4 (trough/recovery) odds are 0.534. The risk is migration: HY OAS is 320bp against a 448bp Phase-2 trigger, SOX is -28.21% against a -30% signpost, and VXN is 28.55 against 35. Rally conditions are 'on' (VIX spike-and-turn with calm credit). Historically about 47.4% of those setups were traps, with typical gains of 10.7% over 17.5 days, against real rallies of 32.4% over 106.5 days (computed). Today's rate shock is a classic Phase-1-to-2 catalyst if it persists. Anthropic's potentially roughly $100B IPO is the clearest froth marker in the primary market (analyst estimate of the IPO froth gauge). Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December FOMC: a 25bp hike is the most likely outcome (inference). The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% in late October with two dissents in favour of an immediate hike, and markets still price a December hike. Warsh has named December as a decision point but refuses to pre-commit, and today's +14.37bp move in the 2Y is consistent with the market leaning toward a hike.

~1 YEAR

Over about a year, a moderately hawkish, data-dependent path (inference): one analyst sees markets pricing about 1.5 more hikes in 2027, with roughly one in the first half. Warsh's long-standing preference for a smaller Fed balance sheet is our inference from his prior public record and was not re-verified in this run's sources. The FOMC is also moving to a 'six-plus-two' meeting schedule.

Warsh has kept to a script of optionality. He 'won't prejudge the rest of 2026', named October and December as the key decision points, and handed the decision back to incoming data. At the October hold the Fed upgraded growth from 'solid' to 'strong'. One analyst called the hike 'postponed but not abandoned'. Rate-hike bets have barely moved on his rhetoric, which suggests the market reads his words through the data (sticky core near 3%, oil at 95.8). Flagged inference: with inflation breadth high and the labor market tight (claims 200k), a hold in December would likely require a clear growth or credit shock. One source cites an earlier policy range of 3.5–3.75%, which conflicts with the 3.75–4.00% figure; verify against the Fed's statement.

Descriptive regime read, not advice and not a recommendation to trade. Rule results are simulations on one market history (3x daily returns rebuilt from index data, 1-day lag, costs), and the exits (+10% target, 5-day pause) were chosen after testing a few values on that same history, so treat them as in-sample. The trend+vol engine is a drawdown control, not proven timing skill (trendvol TRENDVOL.md § CORRECTION).
